children: The industrial sector looked unstoppable for much of this year, and that's what makes its August drop so concerning.

The State Street Industrial Select Sector SPDR exchanged-traded fund has fallen more than 5% over the past two weeks, after climbing 17% from January through July. It has declined in eight of the last 10 sessions, and closed at or near the daily range lows in nine of them-a clear sign of persistent selling pressure. It brings to mind the old adage "amateurs open the market and pros close it."
The technical signals suggest that now might not be a time to jump into the sector, with Norfolk Southern being one notable exception.

More worrisome is that the mid-August breakout above the $184.52 double-bottom pivot that quickly failed-that's a red flag, given that the strongest breakouts typically work right away. Two bearish shooting stars and a doji between Aug. 5 and 17 suggested price fatigue. The ETF has now closed below its 50-day simple moving average for seven straight sessions and appears increasingly likely to test its 200-day SMA, similar to what occurred on March 30. Another sign of weakness: The fund has been a notable laggard since the beginning of March, as illustrated by its ratio chart versus the S&P 500.
The State Street Industrial Select Sector SPDR ETF was trading around $175 Monday.

Over the past month, airline stocks have been among the biggest culprits behind the ETF's drop, as crude oil prices, while off their highs, remain elevated. Shares of Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are both down more than 10% over the past month. In the week ending July 10, both stocks completed bearish evening star patterns. However, the technical picture is beginning to improve, with both stocks approaching potential buy points and appearing to form double-bottom bases as they test their upward-sloping 200-day SMAs.

Perhaps more troubling is the price action in the trucking stocks. Undoubtedly, the group has been hit hard by diesel prices, which have doubled over the past year, and the charts reflect the deterioration in the group. J.B. Hunt Transport Services was rejected at the very round $300 level, forming a spinning top in the week ending July 17. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, meanwhile, lost one-third of its value during the final two weeks of July following an ill-received earnings reaction. Last week, the stock recorded a bearish death cross, while its ratio chart shows how significantly it has lagged behind J.B. Hunt since March.

Interestingly, C.H. Robinson is another name that failed quickly after breaking out from a cup base at the $200 level on July 16, subsequently forming a bear flag. Resistance now appears near $150, a former area of major support that produced sharp reversals on Feb. 12 and May 14. A decisive break below that level could open the door to further downside, and a fill of the Oct. 29, 2025 gap near $127 looks plausible by year-end.
C.H. Robinson Worldwide was trading around $151 Monday.

Perhaps companies are simply shifting more freight to the rails. Intermodal transportation, which favors rail over trucking to move goods over longer distances, can lower costs through greater fuel efficiency while also reducing emissions. Or perhaps the weakness is more company-specific. FedEx trades just 4% below its 52-week high, while United Parcel Service remains 14% below its annual peak.

Looking at the rail names, Norfolk Southern Corporation stands out as a possible buy. Over the past year, candlestick patterns have played a pivotal role in identifying near-term lows, beginning with a doji on Sept. 10, 2025. A bullish harami appeared on March 20 at the 200-day SMA, followed by a bullish morning star at the same key long-term moving average on June 22. More recently, a bull flag has taken shape, beginning with a bearish evening star on July 27. A move above $353 could trigger a quick advance toward $400 by year-end, representing 15% upside from current levels. Remain bullish above $335.
Norfolk Southern stock was trading around $344 Monday.
